title: Different Yet the Same
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: In another prelude to his forthcoming book on instructional paradoxes, Paul Kirschner tackles the apparent tension between two obviously true claims: students differ enormously (interests, pace, talent) and yet all learners share the same underlying cognitive architecture (the same three-store memory system). He resolves the tension with a digestive-system analogy: everyone's digestion works the same way and follows the same basic nutritional principles, yet no single diet is right for everyone, and in extreme cases diet must be fully personalised without ever violating those shared underlying principles. Applied to teaching, this means well-established instructional frameworks -- Rosenshine's principles, Sweller's cognitive load theory, Mayer's multimedia learning theory -- genuinely apply to essentially all learners and should be used, but not as a rigid, identical checklist; the number of interventions, amount and spacing of practice, task complexity, and level of scaffolding must all vary by prior knowledge and expertise. He extends the analogy to a track-and-field coach training athletes across every event and body type using the same core training principles (exertion-then-rest, interleaving) while varying the specific parameters per athlete, then works through several of Rosenshine's principles explicitly adapted for younger versus older learners as a worked example.
points: Kirschner's digestive-system analogy resolves what looks like a genuine contradiction (all learners are the same / all learners are different) by separating shared underlying mechanism from necessarily personalised application.

His explicit list of what varies by learner -- number of interventions, spacing and amount of practice, task complexity relative to expertise, and extraneous cognitive load from a given technique -- turns the abstract sameness/difference tension into specific, adjustable teaching levers.

The track-and-field coaching analogy extends the argument to a second concrete domain (physical training, not just diet), reinforcing that shared core principles plus individualised parameters is a general pattern, not a one-off metaphor.

His worked comparison of Rosenshine's principles for younger vs. older learners (fun review activities vs. structured quizzes; hands-on scaffolds vs. templates and outlines) gives teachers a direct, applied model for translating one universal framework across age groups.
quotes: They have different interests, learn at different speeds, have different talents, and so on. This is indisputable and means that we must take note of these differences and not try to teach all learners in exactly the same way.
This architecture consists of three interrelated and connected information stores or memories and this is the same for all learners.
Let’s look at the digestive system. All our digestive systems are essentially the same, and because of this, all of the basic principles involved in eating and health are the same for all people.
And there's no one perfect diet for everyone. Some people need larger portions than others, some people need different mixtures of foods and nutrients than others.
They're not a checklist for everyone, every day in all lessons. The number of interventions and their nature will vary with prior knowledge and aptitude.
Task complexity and thus its intrinsic cognitive load, differs with expertise; something complex for a novice is simple for an ‘expert’ and vice versa.
Teachers also need to do this. They have to adapt proven general principles to groups of learners or even individuals.
